newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US, fears mount ahead of G7 mtg.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US, fears mount ahead of G7 mtg.

text.p: The dollar ended higher against the mark but modestly weaker versus the yen on Friday as fears mounted that the G7 would take steps to slow the dollar's recent rise against the Japanese currency at its upcoming summit meeting.

Several foreign officials, including members of the Bundesbank and U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, suggested on Friday that the dollar's recent surge against the yen would be a key topic of conversation at the Berlin gathering, scheduled to begin on February 8.
Their remarks led traders to take profits in the dollar, which has risen by over four percent against the yen since the beginning of the year.
"When you hear all these comments you begin to wonder whether the G7 is more concerned about the dollar's rise than people had thought," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International.
"While it's unlikely that the G7 comes out with any statement which would tend to encourage a reversal in exchange rates, the risk is that they could temper it which makes traders nervous," he added.

The dollar ended the day at 121.40/45 yen, down from 121.55/65 yen at the open and 121.80/85 at Thursday's close. Against the mark, the dollar edged higher to close at 1.6383/88 against 1.6340/50 at the open.

On Friday, a wire service quoted Guntram Palm, a council member of Germany's Bundesbank, as saying the dollar's recent rise against the yen would be a "major topic" at the meeting, overshadowing discussions on European Economic and Monetary Union.
His remarks were echoed by Bundesbank Vice President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum and Britain's Clarke, who both said dollar strength would be a focus at the summit.
"You're seeing a very calculated and orchestrated attempt to slow the dollar's rise against the yen down," said Paul Park, a trader at Mellon Bank.
Also weighing on dollar/yen was ongoing selling of sterling by Japanese investors and reports of a large hedge fund selling dollars for yen.

Limiting the dollar's losses against the yen, and boosting it against the mark on Friday, was a Commerce Department report which showed that the U.S. economy grew at a surprisingly strong 4.7 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter.

The strong growth figures also helped the dollar maintain its overseas gains against the British pound, which was plagued again by diminishing hopes for an interest rate rise ahead of upcoming U.K. elections.
Sterling ended the session at $1.6025/35, only slightly lower than its opening rate of $1.6030/40, but substantially off Thursday's close of $1.6135/45.
Elsewhere, the dollar ended higher at 1.4236/41 Swiss francs versus 1.4185/95 at the open. The dollar ended a tad lower at Canadian $1.3470/75 against C$1.3484/89 in early dealings.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7618/23 versus $0.7620/30 at the open.
